# Report: Chalmers, "Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness"

**1. The question, frozen.** The paper answers several, so I take the one its title and opening make central: *why is conscious experience hard to explain — why do the reductive, function-explaining methods of cognitive science and neuroscience fail here, when they work on genes, life and learning?* That is a "why can't it happen" question — a block. Its range is meant to be every physical or functional account, present and future. A second question rides along (*what kind of account could succeed?*) and a third (*what is it?*). I keep them apart, because a part can be tight for one and idle for another.

**2. The explanation in parts.** P1 the easy/hard split; P2 the conceptual asymmetry (for functionally definable things, explaining the function *is* explaining the thing); P3 the further question, *why is the function accompanied by experience at all?*; P4 the conceivability premise (any physical process is conceivable without experience); P5 therefore experience is not entailed by physical accounts, and reductive methods must fail; P6 extra ingredients all fail (chaos, non-algorithmic processing, quantum, new neurophysiology); P7 the vitalism disanalogy; P8 take experience as fundamental; P9 psychophysical principles as new basic laws; P10 structural coherence; P11 organizational invariance; P12 the double-aspect view of information.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| P1 easy/hard split | **Held** by the sorting job: it must place Crick & Koch, Baars, Edelman, Dennett, Jackendoff correctly, and does. |
| P2 conceptual asymmetry | **Held** by the same job. Caution: the test that sorts a problem as easy is *functionally definable*, which is close to the test that sorts it as reducible. |
| P3 the further question | **Held**: every part below is held in place by it. |
| P4 conceivability premise | **Borrowed**: its defence is deferred to a footnote (Chalmers 1996, a posteriori necessity). Nothing here tests it. |
| P5 no entailment, so no reduction | **Held if** P4 holds. The job is real; the premise under it is in doubt, and the settling test is named at the end of this report. |
| P6 extra ingredients rejected | **Held**: it kills a family of named rivals (Penrose, Hameroff), and says what should *not* matter — more neurophysiological detail. |
| P7 vitalism disanalogy | **Held if**: it leans on P2/P5. |
| P8 experience as fundamental | **Held if** P5. The Maxwell analogy is **borrowed**: charge earned its place in the equations; Chalmers allows experience may have no function. |
| P9 psychophysical principles | **Loose** as stated — "principles connecting physical and experiential" is nearly a bin. It is saved only by the two gauges below. |
| P10 structural coherence | **Held** by the job of explaining the structure of experience (colour space, visual geometry) without reducing it. See the pull below. |
| P11 organizational invariance | **Held if** an unstated continuity premise holds (see below). |
| P12 double-aspect information | **Unknown**: he says so himself ("more of an idea than a theory"). The test that would settle it: does information-space structure predict anything structural coherence does not?

Where the parts came from: P6, P7 and the case-studies are **fitted** to cases he chose and read; P2 is **built** from how reductive explanation has actually worked; P4 and P12 are **asserted** (P4 with support parked elsewhere); P11 is **built** but leans on an asserted premise.

**4. Whole-explanation checks.** *Flip:* passes — the argument is asymmetric, and had experience turned out functionally explainable, P5 is what he would have been wrong about. *Hunt the answer in the starting points:* P4 is the conclusion's twin ("it is conceivable that it occurs without experience" → "it is not entailed" → "no reduction"); the whole paper's weight sits there. *Add a job:* "no future neuroscience will close the gap" genuinely kills the wait-for-detail rival. *Whose cases:* Koch's own interview quote is strong evidence; Baars is Chalmers' reading, not Baars'. *Pull:* inverted spectra do opposite work in adjacent sections — intelligible in P10 (structure does not exhaust experience), declared nomologically impossible in P11. *Catch-all:* P10 can absorb any correlate by redescribing it as "a mechanism of awareness"; the gauges are inverted spectra and the noticeability of change. *Change list:* his negative claim is tested by thought experiments, not by changes to the world; the one clear "would not matter" half is that more neural detail leaves the hard question open. *What it leaves out:* that modal step is never itself on the list.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** (1) Give P4 a checkable edge: name a case that would show experience *is* entailed by a physical account, then go looking, the way he went looking at Crick and Koch. (2) Supply or drop the continuity premise P11 needs — that experience changes gradually enough along the neuron-to-silicon spectrum for a under-a-tenth swap to span an experiential difference.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. The argument could be tight and still fail if a posteriori necessity holds. Nothing here settles whether experience is physical.

**7. One next step.** Write down, before looking, what would count against P4, then run the case that could break it.
